analysis.one_liner: Strips tax breaks and federal mortgage financing from corporate landlords of single-family homes and taxes their home sales at 100%.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: introduced in October 2024 with 11 Democratic cosponsors, it received no committee vote or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets investors with more than $100 million in assets that buy up single-family homes. It takes away their tax deductions for mortgage interest, insurance, and depreciation, bars Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae from financing their home purchases, and imposes a tax equal to the full sale price on any home they sell. Money raised would go to a trust fund that builds rental housing for the lowest-income families.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and people trying to buy a first home, who today compete with well-financed corporations for a limited supply of single-family houses. The Housing Trust Fund would also gain a new funding stream for rental homes affordable to extremely low-income families.

how_it_helps.text: Denies investors with over $100 million in assets the tax deductions for mortgage interest, insurance, and depreciation on single-family homes of one to four units, removing a benefit smaller landlords do not get the advantage of at this scale [S2].
Imposes an excise tax equal to the entire sale price on any single-family home sold by a covered investor, making it extremely costly for large investors to hold homes for resale profit [S2].

Prohibits Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae from newly purchasing, guaranteeing, or securitizing mortgages where the lender is a large investor, cutting off a federally backed financing channel that lowers corporate landlords' borrowing costs [S2].
Deposits the revenue from the excise tax into the Housing Trust Fund, which funds rental housing affordable to extremely low- and very low-income families, including homeless families [S2].

Exempts newly constructed or substantially rehabilitated homes, federally assisted affordable housing, and an investor's own principal residence, so the penalties fall on the purchase of existing homes rather than on new construction [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations and investment funds with over $100 million in assets that own single-family rental homes. They lose their deductions, lose access to government-backed mortgage financing, and cannot sell a covered home without paying a tax equal to its full sale price.

drawbacks.text: The excise tax equals 100% of the sale price, so a covered investor who tries to sell a home would owe the government the entire proceeds. Critics would say this does not push homes to families — it simply locks the investor in, since selling is economically impossible [S2].

Taking away deductions on millions of investor-owned rentals could raise those owners' costs, and some of that could be passed to tenants as higher rents, at least while the homes stay in investor hands [S2].
The new rules would not take effect until 18 months after enactment, giving large investors a window to restructure holdings before the penalties apply [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The deduction rollback and the ban on federally backed financing for large landlords are reasonably targeted at an affordability problem many families feel directly. The 100% sale tax is a blunt instrument: rather than encouraging large landlords to sell homes to families, it makes selling unaffordable, which could entrench corporate ownership instead of reducing it. The affordable-housing funding stream is real but depends on sales that the tax itself discourages.

outcome.mechanism: The House sent it to the Ways and Means and Financial Services committees; neither took it up, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the bill on October 22, 2024, joined by 10 other House Democrats as original cosponsors [S2].
It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Financial Services Committee, splitting jurisdiction over its tax and housing provisions [S1][S4].
Eleven House Democrats had signed on as cosponsors; no Republicans did [S3].
No committee held a hearing, markup, or vote, and the bill never reached the House floor; the action history shows no activity after the referral [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and all bills not enacted expire [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporate landlords came out ahead: they kept their mortgage-interest and depreciation deductions, their access to federally backed mortgage financing, and faced no tax on selling homes. The Housing Trust Fund received no new funding.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; with Republicans holding the House majority and the committee chairs, the bill had no path to a vote.

industries.note: Companies and funds with over $100 million in assets that own single-family rentals would lose their mortgage-interest, insurance, and depreciation deductions, lose Fannie/Freddie/Ginnie financing that lowers their borrowing costs, and face a 100% tax on any sale. Their business model competes with families for a fixed supply of homes, so their loss is where the bill's benefit to buyers and renters comes from.

industries.industry: Government-sponsored mortgage enterprises (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Ginnie Mae)
industries.note: The bill bars them from newly buying, guaranteeing, or securitizing mortgages made by large investors, shrinking part of their business. Ending that financing channel redirects federally backed credit away from corporate landlord purchases and toward ordinary homebuyers.

Excise-tax revenue would flow to the Housing Trust Fund, which finances rental housing for extremely low- and very low-income families, creating new demand for affordable-housing builders and operators.

The bill exempts homes that are newly constructed or substantially rehabilitated, so large investors can keep deductions when buying new construction. That gives builders a modest sales advantage, and the resulting new supply adds homes — though investors holding them as rentals does nothing for aspiring buyers.
